flashcards.q: What does REST actually buy you that GraphQL and gRPC don't, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Free HTTP-level caching and universal tooling: a GET with a stable URL can be cached by any intermediary (CDN, browser, proxy) with zero extra work. GraphQL's POST-body queries and gRPC's binary framing don't get this for free.

flashcards.q: How much smaller is Protobuf than the equivalent JSON payload, roughly?
flashcards.a: Commonly 2-5x smaller on the wire, plus gRPC gets HTTP/2 multiplexing and native deadline propagation that plain JSON-over-HTTP doesn't have by convention.

flashcards.q: What is the GraphQL N+1 problem and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: A naive resolver for a list field issues one DB query per parent item (N) plus the original list query (1). DataLoader batches all requests for the same field type issued within one event-loop tick into a single WHERE id IN (...) query.

flashcards.q: GraphQL has no default depth or cost limit. What two controls must you add, and what do they each catch?
flashcards.a: Depth limiting (reject queries nested past ~5-10 levels) catches deep nesting attacks. Cost/complexity analysis (assign per-field cost, scaled by list-size arguments, reject over a budget e.g. 1000 points) catches wide queries that depth limiting alone misses.

flashcards.q: What HTTP status code does GraphQL return on a partial resolver failure, and why does that matter?
flashcards.a: 200 OK, with an `errors` array alongside partial `data`. It matters because clients can't rely on status-code checking alone and must inspect the errors array explicitly.

flashcards.q: WebSocket vs SSE: what's the precise deciding question?
flashcards.a: Does the client need to send data on the same low-latency channel mid-stream? If yes, WebSocket (full duplex). If the client only receives (ticker, notifications, LLM token streaming), use SSE -- it's plain HTTP with automatic reconnect built into the EventSource spec.

flashcards.q: Why does SSE pass through corporate proxies and CDNs more easily than WebSocket?
flashcards.a: SSE is a normal long-lived HTTP GET response, so it flows through ordinary HTTP infrastructure. WebSocket requires an `Upgrade: websocket` handshake that many proxies/firewalls don't handle correctly, and needs connection affinity at the load balancer.

flashcards.q: What three things must a webhook receiver implement that the provider does NOT guarantee for you?
flashcards.a: Retry-safe idempotency (dedupe by provider event ID, atomic insert-or-ignore), signature verification (HMAC over the raw body before trusting the payload), and handling of out-of-order delivery (no ordering guarantee across retries).

flashcards.q: Long-polling vs plain polling -- what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: Plain polling: client requests at a fixed interval, gets an immediate (possibly empty) response every time. Long-polling: server holds the request open (commonly 20-30s) until data is ready or a timeout, then the client immediately reissues -- better latency, but ties up a connection per waiting client.

flashcards.q: Name three concrete cases where a message queue beats any request/response protocol.
flashcards.a: 1) Downstream is unreliable/slow -- queue buffers instead of the caller timing out. 2) Need at-least-once delivery with replay (Kafka retains messages for a configurable window, e.g. 7 days). 3) Fan-out to many consumers at different processing speeds without adding to the producer's latency budget.

flashcards.q: When is a message queue the WRONG tool despite decoupling being attractive?
flashcards.a: When the caller needs a synchronous answer right now to proceed (e.g., render a page). A queue just relocates the wait (polling or holding a connection for the eventual result); it doesn't remove it, and it adds queue operational overhead on top.

flashcards.q: What's the single most common real GraphQL production incident?
flashcards.a: Naive resolver N+1 -- a query that looks fine syntactically fires one DB query per item in a list because DataLoader-style batching wasn't implemented, causing p99 spikes on specific queries.

flashcards.q: gRPC deadlines vs plain HTTP timeouts -- what's the mechanical difference?
flashcards.a: gRPC deadlines propagate as wire metadata through the whole call chain, so a downstream service sees the REMAINING time budget, not a fresh timeout. Plain HTTP has no equivalent unless every hop manually threads a deadline header through the chain.
